  Reference for the translation catalogs, the i18n runtime, non-Latin
  and bidirectional text, and right-to-left layout. Read this before adding a

  that compile are pluralising by concatenation, splicing fragments into a
  sentence, translating at module load or at storage time, nailing a style to a
  physical side, comparing text without normalising it, and translating a string
  that crosses the wire to bitchat.

# Internationalization

How user-facing copy is written, stored, translated and laid out in 35 languages, three of them right to left. The design and its reasons are in [ARCHITECTURE.md section 10](../../docs/spec/ARCHITECTURE.md#10-localization); this card holds the working rules and the do-not-translate list.

| Fact              | Value                                                 |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Languages         | 35, listed in `src/i18n/languages.ts`                 |
| Source catalog    | `src/i18n/locales/en.ts`, hand-written                |
| Catalog format    | `src/i18n/locales/<code>.ts`, flat dotted keys        |
| Right to left     | Arabic, Persian, Urdu. The other 32 are left to right |
| Hardcoded strings | 0, and CI fails on the first one added                |

## Key Files

| Path                                                                    | Holds                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/i18n/index.ts`                                                     | `t` / `useT` / `tPlural`, the catalog registry, device-language resolution, the direction policy           |
| `src/i18n/languages.ts`                                                 | the language table (endonym, direction, script) and `LANGUAGE_ORDER`                                       |
| `src/i18n/plurals.ts`                                                   | CLDR category selection, and `PLURAL_CATEGORIES`, the forms each language needs                            |
| `src/i18n/layout.ts`                                                    | right-to-left helpers React Native has no logical form for                                                 |
| `src/i18n/upper-case.ts`, `src/ui/components/upper-text.tsx`            | `upperCase` in the reading language, and `UpperText` built on it                                           |
| `src/i18n/rich-text.tsx`                                                | `useRichText` / `fillRichText`, for a sentence with a link or a node inside it                             |
| `src/i18n/pseudo.ts`                                                    | the generated `qps-ploc` locale, debug builds only                                                         |
| `src/i18n/locales/types.ts`                                             | `TranslationKey`, `PluralKey`, `CatalogKey` and `PluralForms`, derived from `en.ts`                        |
| `src/utils/message-text.ts`                                             | stored rows: `systemRow` / `messageText`, `systemPreview` / `activityPreview`, `txFailure` / `txErrorText` |
| `src/utils/message-preview.ts`                                          | list-row and bell previews for a message, attachments included                                             |
| `src/utils/format.ts`                                                   | numbers, amounts, dates and `formatBytes`, in the app's language                                           |
| `src/utils/strip-invisibles.ts`, `utf8-budget.ts`                       | `stripInvisibles`, `truncateToUtf8Bytes`                                                                   |
| `src/utils/search-text.ts`                                              | `searchKey`: NFC, isolates stripped, lower-cased                                                           |
| `src/utils/emote.ts`                                                    | the `/hug`, `/slap` and screenshot-notice wire forms                                                       |
| `src/i18n/__tests__/catalog.test.ts`                                    | placeholders, plural sets, `=1`, digits, punctuation, and the protocol tokens                              |
| `scripts/i18n-audit.js`, `i18n-build-locale.js`, `i18n-check-native.js` | the audit, the locale generator, the OS-string check                                                       |

## The Rule

Never write a user-facing string inline. Add a key to `en.ts`, then `T("your.key")` from `useT()` inside a component, or `t("your.key")` outside React. The catalog is what makes every string greppable, reviewable in one diff and consistent in wording.

Completeness is a type. Every locale is annotated `Strings`, which is `Record<TranslationKey, string>` derived from `en.ts`, so a locale missing a key does not compile. There is no runtime fallback and no coverage threshold: adding an English key breaks every incomplete locale at compile time rather than degrading it in front of a user.

## Writing a String

**Placeholders** are named (`{count}`, `{name}`), never positional, because translators reorder sentences. An unfilled one renders as literal `{name}`, so the gap shows in a screenshot.

**Whole sentences, never fragments.** A label, filter name or reason spliced into a sentence cannot agree with it in case or gender, and a translator handed half a sentence cannot reorder it. Give each variant its own whole-sentence key.

**Plurals** go through `tPlural`, never a ternary or a count in a plain string:

```ts
tPlural("mesh.peers_in_range", count); // correct
`${n} peer${n !== 1 ? "s" : ""} in range`; // wrong
```

Selection lives in `plurals.ts`: nine CLDR rule shapes cover all 35 languages, and `plurals.test.ts` checks each against Node's ICU for every integer 0 to 2000. `PluralForms` makes every category but `other` optional, so a Russian catalog carrying only `one` and `other` type-checks and reads "5 сообщение" from five up. `catalog.test.ts` holds every catalog to exactly its language's `PLURAL_CATEGORIES`.

**Exactly one** is its own form. A plural may carry `"=1"`, which `tPlural` checks before the CLDR category, for wording with no number in it ("Someone nearby"). A `one` form must contain `{count}`, because `one` is not "exactly one": Filipino's covers 5, Ukrainian's 21, Hindi's 0. A locale carries `=1` exactly where `en.ts` does; `catalog.test.ts` and the locale generator enforce both rules.

**Upper case** goes through `UpperText` (or `upperCase(text, language)`), never `textTransform: "uppercase"`, which follows no locale on iOS and the device's on Android, never the app's. Turkish needs a dotted İ, and Georgian is left as written.

**A sentence with a link or a node inside it** uses `useRichText`, or `fillRichText` where a hook cannot run. Never concatenate `<Text>` fragments.

## Translate at Display, Never at Load or Storage

```ts
const SCOPES = { tag: t("chat.scope.mesh") }; // wrong: frozen at import
const SCOPES = { tagKey: "chat.scope.mesh" }; // correct
```

Three shapes of one bug, all of which compile:

- **Module scope.** Evaluated once at import, so it holds whichever language the app started in.
- **A memo without the translator in its deps.** `useMemo(..., [Colors])` calling `t()` never recomputes on a language change. Use the `T` from `useT()` inside it and list it.
- **A row written to MMKV.** Storage outlives the language it was written in, so a persisted row carries a key and its variables and translates on render.

`npm run i18n:audit` fails on the first two. For the third, build the row with the helper that writes the key, its variables and a plain fallback together:

- a chat row: `...systemRow(key, vars)`, read back with `messageText`
- a bell entry: `systemPreview`, or `messagePreviewEntry` for a message preview
- a wallet failure: `txFailure(key, vars)` for Airhop's words, `txFailureVerbatim(text)` for a mint's, read back with `txErrorText`

## Non-Latin and Bidirectional Text

**Isolates.** `interpolate` wraps every substituted value in a first-strong isolate, so a right-to-left name inside a left-to-right sentence cannot drag the punctuation around it to the wrong side. It first strips the value with `stripInvisibles`: controls, bidi embeddings, overrides and isolates, zero-width space, the word joiner and tag characters, so a value cannot close its own isolate or reverse the sentence after it. ZWNJ (U+200C) and ZWJ (U+200D) survive, since Persian spelling and emoji sequences need them; any stripping of your own must keep them too. Announced nicknames and received file names go through the same function on arrival. Two things not to undo:

- Do not concatenate `t()` output with a value. Use a placeholder, or the wrap never happens.
- The isolates are display machinery. Strip them with `stripIsolates` before comparing or indexing into `t()` output (`searchKey` does), and before the text leaves the screen: anything sent to a peer, shared to another app, used as a mint memo or stored as a row's plain `text`. `systemRow` strips its fallback already.

**A line built only from values**, such as `"{sender}: {preview}"`, has no strong character of its own, since isolates are skipped when a paragraph picks its direction, so it falls back to left to right and an Arabic row reads backwards around its colon. Lead it with `directionMark` from `layout.ts`.

**Word boundaries** are not `\s` or `[.,!?;:]`. Japanese writes `。`, Arabic `،`, Hindi `।`, Burmese `။`. Match with `[^\p{L}\p{N}_]` and the `u` flag.

**Comparisons** normalise both sides with `.normalize("NFC")`. Two keyboards emit the same accented character differently, and Vietnamese and Korean bite hardest.

**Cutting text** to a byte budget uses `truncateToUtf8Bytes`, never `.slice()`. It counts UTF-8 bytes rather than UTF-16 units, and backs off a trailing combining mark or joiner, which a raw cut orphans in every Indic and South-East Asian script.

**Digits** are Latin everywhere, grouping is not. Hindi and Tamil group by lakh, Georgian by thin space, and `formatNumber` handles both. A catalog may not write its own numerals. `toLocaleString` and its date and time siblings are banned by eslint: they read the device locale, not the app's language.

**The monospace face** is for machine data only. JetBrains Mono covers Latin, Greek and Cyrillic and no other script shipped. A value built from a formatter or a constant may be mono; a value that comes through a catalog key is prose, number or not. `APP_VERSION` is mono, `"Version {version}"` is prose.

## Right to Left Layout

- Logical properties only: `marginStart`, `paddingEnd`, `borderTopStartRadius`, and `start` / `end` for position. Eslint rejects the physical margin, padding and border sides and `textAlign: "left" | "right"`; `left` and `right` positions are not linted, so they are on the reviewer.
- `textAlign` has no logical end in React Native. Use `textAlignEnd` from `layout.ts`, and `"auto"` for the leading edge.
- Text a person wrote aligns by its own direction, not the UI's: `contentTextAlign(text)`, where the first letter decides (the Unicode paragraph rule). iOS and Android otherwise disagree about a message running against the UI.
- Directional glyphs do not mirror themselves. Use `chevronForward`, `chevronBack`, `arrowForward`, `arrowBack`. `arrow-up-right` means outward and stays put.
- Swipe actions go through `trailingSwipeActions`, since the swipeable names its panels by physical side.
- A header title needs `flexGrow` as well as `flexShrink`, or it ellipsizes with free space beside it.
- `layout.ts` and `radar-view.tsx` are the two eslint exemptions. The radar is a polar plot of physical space and must never mirror.

## Which Language Renders

- On the default "system" preference, the app language is the first shipped language in the phone's whole preferred-language list: `getLocales()` from `expo-localization`, resolved by `languageForTags`. A Catalan reader with Spanish second gets Spanish. It is re-sampled on every foreground edge (`refreshDeviceLanguage`).
- Direction is fixed at process start, so a right-to-left switch applies on the next launch, and until then the UI stays in a language that fits the frame. `initI18n()` reads `I18nManager.isRTL` and the stored `frameLanguage` rather than assuming the wanted direction is in force, because on a first launch it is not. `App` raises the restart notice through `translatorFor`, in the language being waited for.

## What Never Gets Translated

These cross the wire, derive an identity or are quoted, so a translated variant is an interop or legal bug rather than a cosmetic one. `catalog.test.ts` enforces the protocol tokens and proper nouns; the audit's `SKIP_FILES` keeps the file-level entries out of the catalog.

| Thing                               | Where                                                                  | Why                                                                                         |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Adjective and noun word lists       | `src/utils/username.ts`                                                | Identity derivation. One peer resolves to one name everywhere                               |
| Transmitted `/hug` and `/slap` text | `src/utils/emote.ts`, `message-thread.tsx`                             | bitchat matches the English substrings; the verbs never enter a catalog                     |
| Transmitted screenshot notice       | `screenshotNotice` in `src/utils/emote.ts`                             | `* name took a screenshot *`, byte for byte bitchat-ios's. Received, it becomes a keyed row |
| Command and link tokens             | `/hug`, `/slap`, `/who`, `/msg`, `airhop://`, `npub1`                  | Matched by a parser, so verbatim in prose. Translate the hint instead                       |
| Channel names and geohashes         | `#bluetooth`, cell ids                                                 | Protocol identifiers, verbatim inside translated prose                                      |
| Proper nouns                        | Airhop, bitchat, Nostr, Cashu, Lightning, Tor, GitHub, Ed25519, X25519 | "Lightning" and "Tor" are ordinary words in most of these languages                         |
| Nicknames, group names, notices     | everywhere                                                             | User content                                                                                |
| Licence texts                       | `src/data/licenses.ts`                                                 | Quoted verbatim                                                                             |
| Terms and Privacy clauses           | `terms-screen.tsx`, `privacy-screen.tsx`                               | English is authoritative. The reader chrome around them is translated                       |
| Mint and relay error strings        | wallet, nostr                                                          | Authored by a remote server, stored with `txFailureVerbatim`                                |

## Adding a Language

1. Give it a row in `LANGUAGES` and the `LanguageCode` union (`languages.ts`, mirrored in `landing/src/i18n/languages.ts`), its rule in `plurals.ts` and `PLURAL_CATEGORIES`, and a `settings.language.<code>` key. All 35 shipped languages already have these.

2. Write the translation as a flat `{ key: text }` map plus a `plurals` map carrying exactly the CLDR categories the language uses, then:

   ```bash
   node scripts/i18n-build-locale.js <code> <translations.json>
   ```

   Key order, section markers and escaping come from `en.ts`. It writes nothing unless every key is present and none is extra, no string is empty, placeholders match English, plural categories and `=1` are right, protocol tokens and proper nouns survived, and no character belongs to a script the language does not write in. The result is a normal hand-editable catalog.

3. Add one line to `REAL` in `index.ts`, with its import. `CATALOGS`, the shipping gate and `catalog.test.ts` all read from it.

4. Translate the strings the OS renders, which it picks by device language rather than by the in-app picker:

   - `ios/Airhop/<code>.lproj/InfoPlist.strings` for the permission dialogs, also listed in `project.pbxproj` and `knownRegions`
   - `android/app/src/main/res/values-<qualifier>/strings.xml` for the foreground-service notification
   - the BCP-47 tag in `res/xml/locales_config.xml`, or Android 13's per-app picker cannot offer the language

   `npm run i18n:native` fails on anything missing, extra or unwired.

## Commands

| Command                          | Does                                                                   |
| -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run i18n:audit`             | hardcoded strings, worst file first. Also fails on frozen translations |
| `npm run i18n:audit -- --list`   | every hit with a line number                                           |
| `npm run i18n:audit -- --unused` | catalog keys nothing references                                        |
| `npm run i18n:audit -- --max 0`  | the CI ratchet                                                         |
| `npm run i18n:native`            | `.lproj`, `values-*` and `locales_config.xml` against the shipped set  |
| `npm run verify:invisibles`      | control characters and bidi overrides in source                        |

The audit is a heuristic, and what it deliberately does not read sits in three lists in `scripts/i18n-audit.js`, each entry with its reason: `SKIP_FILES` (whole files, such as the word lists and legal copy), `IGNORE` (literals that look like copy, such as the `/slap` payload and the screenshot notice) and `IDENTIFIERS` (capitalised words compared in code, such as the NUT-04 quote states). Keep `IDENTIFIERS` narrow: every entry is a word the audit stops reading, so a label spelled the same way slips past.

Set the picker to `qps-ploc` on a debug build to read the pseudolocale: every string accented, bracketed, and padded past the longest real translation of the same key. A screen that holds there holds in all 35.

## What Not to Do

- Write a user-facing string inline.
- Pluralise with `n === 1 ? "" : "s"` at a call site, put a count in a plain string, or leave `{count}` out of a `one` form.
- Splice a translated fragment into another sentence, or change a translated string's case with `textTransform`.
- Call `t()` at module scope, inside a memo without the translator in its deps, or when writing to a store.
- Send, share or store `t()` output without `stripIsolates`.
- Use `marginLeft`, `left`, `textAlign: "right"`, or `toLocaleString` anywhere.
- Compare, slice or match text without normalising it first.
- Set translated prose in `FontFamily.mono`, or a catalog number in anything but Latin digits.
- Translate anything in the table above.
- Ship a language whose catalog is not complete.
